question: Why do you want to study petroleum engineering specifically, rather than a broader engineering degree?
lookingFor: A specific, informed reason for choosing petroleum engineering over a general engineering path, grounded in real interest rather than salary alone.

bullets: Name the specific pull of the field, not just engineering in general
Show you understand what the degree actually covers, day to day
Avoid framing the answer purely around pay or job security
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I looked into general engineering first, but what pulled me toward petroleum specifically was a school trip to a refinery where an engineer walked us through how a well's pressure data actually decides drilling decisions. I liked that it sits right at the meeting point of geology, fluid mechanics, and real economic stakes, which felt more grounded than pure theory. Since then I have read into reservoir characterisation and it only confirmed that this is the specific problem-solving I want to spend my degree on, not engineering in the abstract.

commonMistakes: Answering as if any engineering degree would do
Focusing only on high starting salaries
Vague statements like wanting to work with energy with no specifics
followUps: What part of the curriculum are you most looking forward to?

question: Why do you want to study petroleum engineering at our university in particular?
lookingFor: Specific, researched reasons tied to this program's labs, faculty, or industry links, not generic praise.

bullets: Reference a specific facility, module, or faculty research area
Connect it to a concrete personal interest or project
Show awareness of what distinguishes this program from others
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Your department has a drilling fluids lab that final years actually run experiments in, and I want a course where I am handling core samples and mud rheology myself rather than only reading about them. I also read a paper from one of your reservoir engineering professors on waterflood optimisation, which lines up with a school project I did modelling simple fluid displacement. Beyond the facilities, your program's strong placement links with operators mean the degree is built with a clear route into the industry, which matters to me.

commonMistakes: Praise generic enough to apply to any university
Citing rankings with no specific detail
Not knowing any actual course content or faculty
followUps: What would you want to get involved with outside the classroom here?

subtopic: Origin of interest and wider reading
question: What first got you interested in petroleum engineering, and what have you read or explored since then?
lookingFor: A credible origin story backed by genuine follow-up reading or exploration beyond the initial spark.

bullets: Give an honest, specific starting point for the interest
Name real reading, videos, or resources engaged with since
Show what that reading actually taught, not just that it happened
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: My interest started with a documentary about the Deepwater Horizon investigation, which sounds like an odd place to start, but it made me realise how much engineering judgement sits behind every drilling decision. That sent me down a rabbit hole of reading about well control and blowout preventers, and I later worked through parts of an introductory reservoir engineering textbook a family friend lent me. What stuck with me most was learning how much of the field is about managing uncertainty in data you can never fully see underground.

commonMistakes: Claiming interest with no concrete origin or example
Naming a book or article without being able to discuss its content
Only mentioning family pressure or job prospects as the origin
followUps: What was the most surprising thing you learned from that reading?

question: What experience have you had that gave you real insight into what petroleum engineering involves, and what did you learn from it?
lookingFor: Genuine exposure to the field, however small, with reflection on what it revealed about the actual work.

bullets: Describe a specific experience: internship, site visit, competition, or project
Explain what it taught about the realities of the work
Connect the insight to why the degree still appeals
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I spent a week shadowing a reservoir engineer at a small operator near where I live, and most of my time was actually spent watching them argue with a geologist over how to interpret an ambiguous seismic section. It taught me that petroleum engineering is far less about turning valves and far more about making confident decisions from incomplete data, working closely with other disciplines. That uncertainty did not put me off, it made the field more interesting, because it means the maths and the judgement both matter.

commonMistakes: Describing exposure with no real reflection on what was learned
Overstating a brief or superficial experience
No connection back to why the degree still appeals afterward
followUps: What would you want to experience next if you had the chance?

question: Given the shift toward renewable energy, why choose a career built around oil and gas?
lookingFor: A mature, realistic view of the industry's future rather than defensiveness or naive dismissal of the transition.

bullets: Acknowledge the transition honestly rather than denying it
Show awareness that hydrocarbons will remain part of the energy mix for years and that skills transfer to areas like carbon capture and geothermal
Explain personal reasoning without sounding defensive
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I do not think oil and gas disappears overnight, global demand still relies heavily on it and someone has to manage that transition responsibly, which is exactly the kind of engineering problem I want to work on. At the same time, I know the skills in this degree, subsurface flow, drilling, reservoir modelling, transfer directly into geothermal energy and carbon capture and storage, both of which I find genuinely interesting. I would rather be inside the industry helping it operate more efficiently and cleanly during this shift than watching from outside.

commonMistakes: Dismissing the energy transition as irrelevant
Sounding defensive or evasive about the question
Showing no awareness of how the skills apply beyond oil and gas
followUps: Which transferable skill from this degree interests you most for the future?

question: Can you explain the difference between porosity and permeability in a reservoir rock?
lookingFor: A clear conceptual grasp of two foundational reservoir properties and why both matter for a well to produce.

bullets: Define porosity as the fraction of void space that can store fluid
Define permeability as the rock's ability to let fluid flow through those spaces
Explain why a rock needs both to be a viable reservoir
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Porosity is how much empty space a rock has to actually hold oil or gas, expressed as a percentage of the rock's total volume. Permeability is different, it is about whether those pore spaces are connected enough to let fluid move through the rock toward a well. A rock can be highly porous but have almost no permeability if the pores are isolated, which is why both properties together, not just one, decide whether a formation is worth producing from.

commonMistakes: Treating porosity and permeability as the same thing
Giving a definition with no explanation of why it matters
Forgetting that pores must be connected for permeability to exist
followUps: Can you think of a rock type that might be porous but not very permeable?

question: In simple terms, what does Darcy's law describe and why is it important in petroleum engineering?
lookingFor: An intuitive explanation of fluid flow through porous media and its practical use in predicting well performance.

bullets: Explain that it relates flow rate to pressure difference, permeability, and fluid viscosity
Convey the intuition, more pressure difference or permeability means faster flow, more viscosity means slower flow
Connect it to a real use, like predicting how fast oil moves toward a wellbore
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Darcy's law says that how fast fluid flows through a rock depends on the pressure difference pushing it, how permeable the rock is, and how thick or viscous the fluid itself is. Intuitively, a bigger pressure drop or a more permeable rock pushes fluid through faster, while a thicker fluid like heavy crude moves more slowly for the same conditions. Engineers use it constantly to estimate how oil will flow toward a wellbore, which underpins everything from well spacing decisions to production forecasts.

commonMistakes: Reciting the formula with no intuitive explanation
Confusing permeability's role with porosity's role
Not connecting it to a practical engineering use
followUps: What would happen to flow rate if the fluid's viscosity doubled?

question: What is the difference between a conventional and an unconventional oil or gas reservoir?
lookingFor: Understanding of the permeability distinction and why unconventional resources need different extraction methods.

bullets: Explain conventional reservoirs have enough natural permeability for fluid to flow to a well on its own
Explain unconventional reservoirs, like shale, are tight and need stimulation such as hydraulic fracturing
Note the broader implications, drilling technique, cost, and often horizontal wells
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A conventional reservoir has rock that is permeable enough that oil or gas flows toward a wellbore fairly naturally once you drill into it, like a traditional sandstone reservoir. An unconventional reservoir, such as shale, holds hydrocarbons but the rock is so tight that fluid barely moves through it on its own, so you need horizontal drilling and hydraulic fracturing to create pathways for the oil or gas to escape. That difference is a big part of why the shale revolution needed new technology rather than just more conventional wells.

commonMistakes: Defining unconventional purely as shale without explaining why
Missing the permeability distinction entirely
Not mentioning that different extraction methods are required
followUps: Why did horizontal drilling make such a difference for shale production?

question: What is hydraulic fracturing, and why is it used?
lookingFor: A clear, correct explanation of the process and purpose, showing awareness it is used to access low permeability rock.

bullets: Describe pumping fluid at high pressure to create fractures in the rock
Explain proppant keeps the fractures open so fluid can flow
State the purpose, creating pathways in low permeability rock like shale
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Hydraulic fracturing involves pumping a fluid, usually water mixed with sand and small amounts of chemicals, into a well at very high pressure to crack open the surrounding rock. The sand, called proppant, wedges into those cracks so they stay open once the pumping stops, creating pathways for oil or gas to flow toward the well. It is used mainly in low permeability formations like shale, where the rock would otherwise be too tight for hydrocarbons to move on their own.

commonMistakes: Describing it vaguely as just injecting chemicals underground
Forgetting the role of proppant in keeping fractures open
Not explaining why it is needed in the first place
followUps: What are some of the environmental concerns raised about this process?

question: Can you explain what upstream, midstream, and downstream mean in the oil and gas industry?
lookingFor: A basic but accurate map of the industry's structure and where petroleum engineers typically sit within it.

bullets: Upstream: exploration and production, finding and extracting hydrocarbons
Midstream: transportation and storage, pipelines, tankers, and terminals
Downstream: refining and distribution to consumers, fuels and petrochemicals
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Upstream is exploration and production, the searching for oil and gas and drilling the wells that bring it out of the ground, which is where petroleum engineers mostly work. Midstream covers getting it from the well to where it is needed, so pipelines, tankers, and storage terminals. Downstream is refining that crude oil into usable products like petrol and plastics and getting them to consumers, which is closer to chemical engineering than petroleum engineering.

commonMistakes: Mixing up midstream and downstream
Not knowing where petroleum engineering itself sits in this chain
Describing only one segment and calling it the whole industry
followUps: Which of these three segments interests you most, and why?

question: What causes a blowout, and how do engineers try to prevent one?
lookingFor: Understanding of pressure imbalance as the root cause and the layered safety systems used to control it.

bullets: Explain a blowout happens when formation pressure exceeds the pressure holding it back, causing an uncontrolled release
Mention drilling mud weight as the primary control and blowout preventers as the mechanical backup
Show awareness this is a safety-critical part of the job, referencing an event if relevant
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A blowout happens when the pressure of fluids in the formation overwhelms the pressure engineers are using to hold them back, so oil, gas, or water surges up the well uncontrolled. Normally drilling mud is weighted carefully to balance that formation pressure, and if that fails, a blowout preventer, a large valve assembly on the wellhead, is meant to seal the well off mechanically. Reading about the Deepwater Horizon incident really brought home to me how many layers of that system have to fail at once for a blowout to actually happen, which is part of why well control is taken so seriously.

commonMistakes: Describing a blowout as simply an explosion with no cause explained
Not mentioning mud weight or blowout preventers
Treating it as a purely mechanical failure with no reference to pressure balance
followUps: Why is mud weight itself a delicate balance to get right?

question: What is a reservoir drive mechanism, and can you name one example of how a reservoir might push oil toward a well?
lookingFor: Awareness that natural reservoir energy, not just pumping, drives initial production, with at least one correct example.

bullets: Define drive mechanism as the natural energy source pushing oil toward the wellbore
Give at least one example, such as solution gas drive, gas cap drive, or water drive
Note that this energy declines over time and affects how production is managed
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A drive mechanism is the natural energy in a reservoir that pushes oil toward the wellbore without any external help, at least initially. One example is solution gas drive, where gas dissolved in the oil comes out of solution as pressure drops and expands, physically pushing oil ahead of it. That energy is finite though, which is part of why reservoir engineers monitor pressure so closely, because once natural drive weakens, you need methods like water injection to keep production going.

commonMistakes: Assuming all production is purely from artificial pumping
Naming a drive mechanism with no explanation of how it works
Not connecting the concept to why reservoir pressure is monitored
followUps: What might an engineer do once natural drive energy starts to weaken?

question: What is enhanced oil recovery, and can you give an example of a method used?
lookingFor: Understanding that primary and secondary recovery leave oil behind, and awareness of at least one EOR technique.

bullets: Explain that primary and secondary recovery typically leave a large fraction of oil in place
Define EOR as tertiary methods used to recover more of that remaining oil
Give an example, such as water flooding, gas injection, or thermal methods like steam injection
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Even after natural pressure and methods like water flooding have done their work, a large share of the oil, often more than half, can still be trapped in the reservoir rock. Enhanced oil recovery is the set of techniques used to get more of that oil out, often by changing the properties of the oil or the rock itself. One example is steam injection in heavy oil reservoirs, where heat lowers the oil's viscosity so it flows more easily toward the well, which I find interesting because it is really a thermodynamics problem as much as a drilling one.

commonMistakes: Confusing EOR with simply drilling more wells
Naming a method with no explanation of the mechanism
Not explaining why EOR is needed at all
followUps: Why might steam injection not be suitable for every type of reservoir?

question: What is drilling mud, and what functions does it serve while drilling a well?
lookingFor: Knowledge that drilling fluid does far more than lubricate, covering pressure control, cooling, and cuttings removal.

bullets: Mention cooling and lubricating the drill bit
Mention carrying rock cuttings up out of the wellbore
Mention controlling formation pressure to prevent influxes
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Drilling mud is the fluid circulated down through the drill string and back up the wellbore while drilling. It cools and lubricates the drill bit, which would otherwise overheat from the friction, and it carries the rock cuttings up to the surface so the hole stays clear. It also does the important job of balancing formation pressure, its weight is carefully controlled so fluids in the rock do not surge into the well uncontrolled.

commonMistakes: Describing it as only a lubricant
Missing the pressure control function entirely
Not knowing it also removes cuttings from the hole
followUps: What might happen if the mud weight were set too low?

question: Why does one reservoir produce mostly oil and another mostly gas, when both formed from similar organic material?
lookingFor: Basic grasp of source rock maturity and phase behavior determining whether hydrocarbons end up as oil or gas.

bullets: Mention that the temperature and depth the source rock experienced affects the type of hydrocarbon generated
Note that greater heat and burial depth tends to crack organic matter into lighter gas rather than oil
Show awareness that pressure and temperature at reservoir conditions also affect the phase found there
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: It largely comes down to how much heat and pressure the source rock experienced over geological time. Organic matter that matures at moderate temperatures tends to generate oil, but if it is buried deeper and gets hotter for longer, those same hydrocarbon chains get cracked into lighter, simpler molecules, which is gas. So two source rocks with similar starting material can end up producing very different fluids depending on their thermal history, which is part of why understanding the geological history of a basin matters so much before drilling.

commonMistakes: Assuming oil and gas come from entirely different source material
No mention of thermal maturity or burial depth
Treating the question as purely a drilling issue rather than a geological one
followUps: What would you expect to find in a source rock that is overmature?

question: What is decline curve analysis, and why is it a useful tool for a petroleum engineer?
lookingFor: Awareness that production rates fall over time in a predictable pattern that can be used to forecast future output.

bullets: Explain that well production rate typically declines over time as pressure and drive energy fall
Note that engineers fit historical production data to a decline pattern to forecast future output
Connect it to a practical use, like estimating recoverable reserves or planning economics
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Once a well starts producing, its rate almost always declines over time as reservoir pressure drops, and decline curve analysis is the method of fitting that historical production data to a mathematical trend to predict how it will keep falling. Engineers use it to estimate how much oil or gas a well will ultimately produce over its life, which feeds directly into decisions about whether further investment in that well is worthwhile. I find it appealing because it turns a messy real-world dataset into something you can actually plan a business decision around.

commonMistakes: Describing it as simply tracking that production goes down with no forecasting element
Not connecting the concept to a real decision it supports
Confusing decline curve analysis with reservoir simulation
followUps: What kind of decision might a company make based on a decline curve forecast?

question: What is wireline logging, and what kind of information does it give an engineer about a well?
lookingFor: Basic understanding that logging tools measure rock and fluid properties down the wellbore to characterise the reservoir.

bullets: Explain that sensors are lowered into the well on a cable to measure rock and fluid properties
Mention at least one property measured, such as resistivity, density, or porosity
Note the purpose, identifying where hydrocarbons are and how much might be present
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Wireline logging is when instruments are lowered into the wellbore on a cable to measure the physical properties of the rock layers around it as they are pulled back up. Different tools measure different things, resistivity logs help distinguish oil or gas from water because hydrocarbons resist electrical current differently, while density and neutron tools help estimate porosity. Together those readings let engineers work out where the hydrocarbons actually are in the well and roughly how much might be recoverable, before committing to full production.

commonMistakes: Confusing wireline logging with seismic surveying
Naming a tool with no explanation of what it measures or why
Not connecting logging to the decision of whether to produce a zone
followUps: Why might resistivity be useful for telling oil apart from water in a formation?

question: What is a Christmas tree in oilfield terms, and what does it do?
lookingFor: Basic knowledge of surface wellhead equipment and its role in controlling production flow.

bullets: Identify it as the assembly of valves and fittings on top of a completed well
Explain its function, controlling and monitoring the flow of fluids out of the well
Note it also provides a safety function, allowing the well to be shut in if needed
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A Christmas tree is the arrangement of valves, gauges, and fittings installed on top of a well once it is ready to produce, named for the way the valves branch out like a tree. Its main job is to control and monitor the flow of oil or gas coming out of the well, letting operators adjust production or shut it down entirely if pressure readings look unsafe. It sits between the reservoir and the surface facilities, so it is really the last point of control before hydrocarbons leave the wellbore.

commonMistakes: Confusing it with a blowout preventer, which serves a different drilling-stage purpose
Describing it with no mention of its control or safety function
Not knowing it is a surface, not downhole, piece of equipment
followUps: How is a Christmas tree different from a blowout preventer?

question: Why is a well lined with casing and cement rather than left as an open hole?
lookingFor: Understanding that casing and cement provide structural support, isolate formations, and prevent contamination.

bullets: Mention structural support, preventing the wellbore from collapsing
Mention zonal isolation, keeping fluids in different rock layers from mixing
Mention protecting freshwater aquifers from contamination by wellbore fluids
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: An open hole through soft or unstable rock can collapse, so steel casing is run in to physically support the wellbore and keep it stable. Cement is then pumped into the space between the casing and the rock, and its main job is zonal isolation, stopping fluids from different layers, like water and oil, from migrating into each other or up the well where they should not be. It also protects shallow freshwater aquifers from anything happening deeper in the well, which is one of the most important integrity and environmental functions in the whole design.

commonMistakes: Mentioning only structural support and missing zonal isolation
Not connecting casing and cement to environmental protection
Describing casing and cement as interchangeable rather than complementary
followUps: What might go wrong if the cement job behind the casing were poorly done?

question: What extra challenges does offshore drilling present compared to onshore drilling?
lookingFor: Awareness of the practical, engineering, and cost differences that water depth and remoteness introduce.

bullets: Mention the added complexity of the water column, riser systems, and subsea equipment
Note higher costs and logistical difficulty of operating far from shore
Mention the added weather, safety, and evacuation challenges of a marine environment
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Offshore adds an entire water column between the rig and the seabed, so you need riser systems and subsea equipment just to connect the surface to the wellhead, which onshore wells simply do not need. Everything is also more expensive and slower, equipment, personnel, and supplies all have to be transported by ship or helicopter, and there is far less room for error given how remote some platforms are. On top of that, weather and sea conditions add real safety and evacuation considerations that onshore operations rarely have to plan around in the same way.

commonMistakes: Only mentioning cost with no technical detail
Not mentioning subsea equipment or riser systems at all
Treating offshore and onshore drilling as essentially identical processes
followUps: What do you think a subsea blowout preventer needs to do differently from a surface one?

question: What is viscosity, and why does it matter for how easily oil can be produced?
lookingFor: Clear understanding of viscosity as resistance to flow and its practical impact on production difficulty.

bullets: Define viscosity as a fluid's resistance to flow
Explain that heavier, thicker oils have higher viscosity and are harder to move through rock and pipes
Give a real-world implication, such as needing heat or dilution to produce heavy oil
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Viscosity is basically how thick a fluid is, or how much it resists flowing, and it matters a lot in petroleum engineering because oils vary enormously in viscosity. A light crude flows fairly easily through rock and up a wellbore, but a heavy, viscous oil moves much more sluggishly, which makes it far harder and more expensive to produce and transport. That is part of why methods like steam injection exist, heating heavy oil lowers its viscosity so it flows well enough to actually be extracted economically.

commonMistakes: Confusing viscosity with density
Defining the term with no practical implication attached
Assuming all crude oil behaves the same way regardless of viscosity
followUps: Besides heating, can you think of another way to reduce a heavy oil's effective viscosity?

question: What is API gravity, and what does a higher or lower value tell you about a crude oil?
lookingFor: Basic familiarity with a standard industry measure and what it implies about oil quality and value.

bullets: Identify it as a measure of how light or heavy a crude oil is relative to water
State that a higher API gravity means a lighter oil, a lower value means a heavier oil
Note the practical implication, lighter oils are generally easier to refine and more valuable
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: API gravity is a scale used to describe how light or heavy a crude oil is compared to water, and it is one of the first things quoted about any oil field. A higher API gravity number means a lighter oil that flows more easily and is generally simpler to refine into products like petrol, while a lower number means a heavier, thicker oil that usually needs more processing. Because of that, lighter, higher API oils typically command a higher market price than heavier grades.

commonMistakes: Not knowing whether higher or lower API means lighter oil
Confusing API gravity with viscosity directly
No mention of the practical or economic implication
followUps: Why might a refinery prefer a lighter crude oil over a heavier one?

question: Why is hydrogen sulfide considered such a serious hazard on some oil and gas sites, and how is it managed?
lookingFor: Awareness of a specific, real safety hazard in the field and the basic precautions used to manage it.

bullets: Explain hydrogen sulfide is toxic even at low concentrations and can be fatal quickly at higher levels
Note it is sometimes present naturally in produced gas, called sour gas
Mention management measures, gas detectors, monitoring, and protective equipment or evacuation procedures
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Hydrogen sulfide, often just called H2S, is extremely toxic even in small concentrations, and at higher levels it can be fatal within minutes, which makes it one of the more serious hazards in the industry. Some reservoirs naturally contain it, which is why that gas is called sour gas, and workers on those sites cannot always smell it once concentrations get dangerously high because it deadens the sense of smell. Sites handle it with continuous gas detectors, strict monitoring protocols, and personal protective equipment, plus clear evacuation procedures if levels spike, because there is very little margin for error with a gas like that.

commonMistakes: Assuming it is dangerous only because of its smell, with no mention it becomes undetectable at high concentrations
Not knowing it occurs naturally in some produced gas
Giving no concrete safety measures used to manage it
followUps: Why do you think H2S detection has to be automated rather than relying on smell alone?

subtopic: Traps and the role of geology
question: What does a petroleum engineer need geology for, and can you describe what a hydrocarbon trap is?
lookingFor: Understanding that geology determines where hydrocarbons accumulate, informing where engineering effort is worth spending.

bullets: Explain that geology identifies where hydrocarbons could plausibly have formed and migrated
Define a trap as a geological structure that stops hydrocarbons migrating further, allowing them to accumulate
Give an example of a trap type, such as an anticline or a fault trap
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Geology is really the starting point of the whole process, it tells you where hydrocarbons might have formed, how they migrated through the subsurface, and crucially, where they might have gotten stuck and accumulated in economic quantities. A trap is a geological structure that stops that migration, usually because permeable rock is sealed off by an impermeable layer above or around it. A classic example is an anticline, where rock layers fold upward into a dome shape, so oil or gas rising through the permeable layer gets caught underneath the impermeable cap rock at the top of the fold.

commonMistakes: Treating geology and petroleum engineering as unrelated disciplines
Defining a trap with no example of a trap type
Confusing a trap with the source rock itself
followUps: What role does the seal, or cap rock, play in making a trap effective?

question: What recent development or trend in the oil and gas industry do you find most interesting, and why?
lookingFor: Genuine engagement with current industry developments beyond textbook knowledge, and an ability to explain why it matters.

bullets: Name a specific, real, and reasonably current trend or technology
Explain the technical or economic reason it matters
Show a personal opinion or curiosity about it, not just a factual recitation
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I have been following the growth of carbon capture and storage projects that repurpose depleted oil and gas reservoirs to store carbon dioxide instead, because the subsurface engineering involved, understanding trap integrity and injection behaviour, is almost identical to what petroleum engineers already do for producing wells. What I find most interesting is that it turns an industry often criticised for emissions into one that could genuinely help manage them, using exactly the skill set this degree teaches. I want to understand more about how injectivity and long-term storage security are modelled, because that feels like where a lot of the field's near-term innovation is actually happening.

commonMistakes: Naming a trend with no explanation of why it is technically interesting
Giving an answer that is out of date or factually incorrect
Reciting a headline with no personal opinion or curiosity attached
followUps: What skills from petroleum engineering do you think transfer most directly to that area?
